Slides: taa as the alphabet's smiley face; 'shuu fii maa fii?' built word by word (shuu = what, fii = in, maa = what/not); 'extra, not on the exam'

jiim review at the board: name, J sound, four forms, two handwriting fonts, dot under

Haa vs English h; naHla (bee) / nakhla (palm tree) / nahla (name); Parker asks whether she exaggerates - yes, for listening practice; real speech is faster
Haa articulation coaching: epiglottis, no vibration, tongue back and relaxed, hand on throat; fog a mirror/glasses; 'Haa' when cold or over hot tea
Book p.49 Listening Exercise 2: Habiib, baHth (research), tabuuH (Haa with sukuun), SabaaH (morning); Habiibi register; gym analogy; jaw still, tongue back

Screen-shared Haa slides: header translated (decks made for heritage speakers); naHiil (thin) vs nakhiil (palm trees); Haliib (milk); Hubuub (grain) vs hubuub (wind); Hidhaa' (shoes); Hibr (ink)
khaa introduced: same shape, dot on top, four forms; Habiibi/Habiibti aside; class copies the forms
Board connecting practice: khaab, bakht (she calls it Egyptian 'luck'), baakh, jiim+khaa; stacking vs the book's climb-up method; Hijaab; dot placement for stacked letters

khaa sound (clearing the throat; soft palate) + kha/khu/khi/akh; khaa slides: khubz, khunfusaa', khizaana, baTTiikh (+ shadda aside), ukhTubuuT (octopus cognate), khayma, khaatim, khawkh (peach vs plum; aw next week; durraaq), nakhiil vs naHiil, khashab, khuDaar, khiyaar, khass (not a house)
taHt 'under' - REQUIRED vocab, written at the board (fatHa + sukuun); takht 'bed' optional; same letters, only the dot differs
Homework Dictation Drill 1 at the board with the Lingco videos: jaab, taaj, juubii, jubab, juthath (Damma not waw), jiib (= jeep; Shami jiib = bring)
Dictation Drill 2 at the board (Parker first): Huut, baHth, Habiib (darling / my darling), [taHt skipped], buuHii, baaHat
Wrap-up: drill 5 and Lingco drill 3 still to do; 'ahlan wa sahlan'

words.meaning: sukuun - the 'no vowel' mark (small circle over a letter)

evidence.quote: [en] now notice here the ha is with the sukun
[en] put the fatha on the Tau and the sukun on the Hau

card_notes: Unit 3 topic. She pointed it out on tabuuH (29:26), baTTiikh (54:46) and taHt (60:38).
She also drilled khaa with sukuun ('with a sukuun: akh', 53:44-53:47).

card_notes: The graded register. She marks words as the 'fuSHa word' when dialects differ (Haafila vs Egyptian otobiis).

letters.notes: jiim, reviewed (it was actually taught 9/8 - she lost track across her three sections): 'the name of the letter is called jiim. Can you guess the sound? J sound' (18:35-18:46); connects both sides, four forms, two handwriting fonts (sharp or curvy tail, 'both works'); 'don't forget the position of the dot. This is very important' (19:32-19:35). The three sisters: 'the position of the dot differentiates between jiim, Haa, and khaa' (47:55-48:01); jiim = one dot UNDER. Board frame board_1325 shows the four jiim forms in print and handwriting.

her_clear_utterances.context: 'the name of the letter is called: jiim' (alone at the end)
the jiim SOUND: 'this word has a j, j, j sound' (Lingco Drill 3 demo)

letters.notes: Haa: 'We're gonna call that letter Haa ... when we transliterate it, it's capital H' (20:35-20:44); 'exactly like the jiim, but it does not have any dot' (21:06-21:11); example word fatHa. SOUND (her coaching, the core of the lesson): 'we call this muscle here epiglottis muscle' (25:44-25:58); 'put your hand on your throat ... if you speak in English you might just feel some vibration, but if you're saying the Haa there will be no vibration, more like air going through here, with some contraction ... you're making a little bit contraction' (25:58-26:31); 'the position of the tongue is a little bit to the back ... relaxed, not contracted' (26:32-26:46); 'you're going up - the contraction is not here, it's here' (27:04-27:10); images: fogging a mirror or glasses before cleaning them, the 'Haa' Arabs make when cold or after a sip of hot sweet tea (27:22-27:52); 'this letter Haa is coming from the middle center of the throat' (31:11-31:17); gym: 'sounding the sounds is exactly like going to the gym ... you didn't use [this muscle] before, so now we need to use it a lot' (29:42-30:00); 'there is no rolling ... no vibration ... it's like you're trying to force air but you're contracting, not all the way' (36:01-36:34). She admits exaggerating it when modelling (Parker's question): 'I'm saying it forcefully, a little bit more than usual, in order to help you develop your listening skills. When we speak, we speak faster ... because you know fatHa, you know the word' (24:06-24:50). Vowels: 'Ha' and 'Hi' are easier, 'Hu' (Damma/waw) is harder (34:16-34:23, 38:59-39:06). Board shows حاء and H.

khaa: 'Very similar to the jiim and the Haa except for the position of the dot. This one doesn't go under, it goes at the top' (40:47-40:59); four forms named independent / initial / middle / connecting-ending (41:00-41:14). Sound: 'That is easier ... it's like clearing your throat, so we all did that sound before' (52:38-52:45); 'The khaa is coming from, they call it the soft palate. At the top, it's like the back of your throat, at the top' (53:13-53:21); versus Haa, which is lower ('you're hitting above where you're supposed to hit ... that's the next letter', 32:14-32:22); 'With a khaa, there is some little bit of vibration, but up' (58:06-58:10). Syllable drill kha / khu / khi / akh (53:26-53:47): 'This is easier' / 'This is much easier'.

taa as the alphabet's smiley face: 'the Arabic alphabet is so friendly, it even has a smiley face. So the taa, it looked like a smiley face. This is your first slang' (2:33-2:45; slide slide_0152 shows a big ت). Named again when connecting taHt: 'which taa? ... put the fatHa on the taa' (60:29-60:38).

her_clear_utterances.context: 'so the taa, it looked like a smiley face'

letters.notes: alif named in the khaa connecting exercises: 'which alif? connecting ... because khaa connects to the left'; 'baa connects to the right but alif does not connect to the left, so we need the independent one' (45:18-45:34, 47:38-47:45).

her_clear_utterances.context: 'but alif does not connect to the left'

letters.notes: baa named in the connecting exercises ('which baa? independent') and for jiib: 'we say jiib with a baa' - Arabic has no p, English p becomes b (69:05-69:16). Shadda demo: 'instead of saying ba, you would say bb' (55:04).

her_clear_utterances.context: 'I'm writing a baa and then a jiim'

letters.notes: waaw as the long-u letter: 'here with a waw' (Huut) and the Damma-vs-waw spelling trap in dictation: 'we needed the Damma, not the waw' (67:19-67:21); 'Some students might think it's a waw. No, it's quick' (65:45-65:55). In khawkh the waw is the diphthong she will teach next week.
Only incidental: in the juthath correction she stressed '-thath ... the first thaa has the fatHa' (67:21-67:26).

unresolved: bakht (بَخْت, 'luck') - built on the board at 46:25-46:53 (ب + خ + ت); she said 'the word becomes bakht, means luck; in Egyptian they use it. We use a different one in Syria, or even FuSHa is a different one' (2812.8-2822.4). LEFT OUT of words under the no-Egyptian rule even though it is Alif Baa Listening Exercise 3 #4 - Parker's call.
otobiis ('bus') at 1988.5-1989.2 - she labelled it Egyptian and gave Haafila as the FuSHa word; not listed (note that Lingco's Unit 5 vocab lists أوتوبيس for formal and shaami too).
biddak (بِدَّك 'you want', Shami) - only the Arabic pass has it, inside her 'jiib jiib' joke at 4169.8-4170.5 ('بيدك جيب جيب جيب'); not listed as a word.

Six Haa slides (Halwaa, naHla, HiSaan, Haafila, Hadiid, fallaaH) were shown only on the room projector (31:00-37:06); the camera caught the pictures, not the text. Their spellings are standard vowelling from own knowledge; the slide may differ in which vowels it printed.

kiif il-Haal and kiifak/kiifik (74.7-77.1) are inferred from the Teams caption 'Kifilhal, kifhalla, kifik'; the English pass only heard 'kifhalik' once. Low confidence on both the spans and the exact forms.
